blocks.text: 1. Cohen Kappa
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061511-836892624.png

Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score, along with the ROC Curve, AUC, Log Loss, and Precision-Recall Curve, all covered throughout this module, each address a genuine, specific weakness in the metrics that came before them, yet none of them directly corrects for one final, subtle but important factor: how much apparent agreement between a model's predictions and the true labels could have arisen purely by chance alone, with no genuine learning involved at all.

Cohen Kappa closes out this module by correcting for exactly that, measuring genuine agreement between predictions and true labels after explicitly subtracting out whatever level of agreement pure random chance, given the actual class proportions in the data, would already be expected to produce on its own. This makes it a genuinely different, complementary lens on classifier quality from every metric already covered, and a fitting way to close this module's full toolkit.
2. The Core Insight: Chance Agreement Is Real

blocks.alt: The Core Insight: Chance Agreement Is Real
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061512-766558759.png

Even a classifier making purely random, uninformed predictions, with no genuine relationship to the input features at all, will sometimes agree with the true label, purely by coincidence. This effect becomes especially pronounced whenever one class is significantly more common than another, exactly the class imbalance concern already covered in depth in the Accuracy topic, since simply guessing the common class often, even at random, will coincidentally match the true label a large fraction of the time.

Raw accuracy, as covered in its own topic, counts this kind of coincidental, chance-driven agreement exactly the same as genuine agreement that reflects real, learned predictive skill, with no way to distinguish between the two. Cohen Kappa exists specifically to make this distinction explicit and quantifiable, separating out how much of a model's apparent agreement with the true labels is genuinely earned versus how much would have happened anyway, purely by chance.
3. The Formula
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061512-810130103.png

Cohen Kappa is built from two quantities. Observed Agreement is exactly what plain accuracy already measures, covered in the Accuracy topic, the fraction of predictions that match their true labels. Expected Agreement is a genuinely new quantity for this module, representing how much agreement would be expected to occur purely by chance, given the actual proportions of each class present in the data.

Cohen Kappa is then computed as Observed Agreement minus Expected Agreement, divided by 1 minus Expected Agreement. This formula directly expresses how much better than pure chance the model's actual agreement genuinely is, as a fraction of the maximum possible improvement over chance that could theoretically be achieved, given that same underlying class distribution.
4. Computing Expected Agreement
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061512-387139250.png

Expected Agreement depends directly on two things for each class: how often the model actually predicted that class overall, and how often that class actually occurred in the true labels overall. For each class, a chance-level agreement rate is computed by multiplying these two proportions together, capturing how often the model would be expected to correctly predict that specific class purely by random coincidence, given how often it tends to predict that class and how often that class genuinely occurs.

Summing these chance-level rates across every class in the problem produces the overall Expected Agreement value. A dataset with one heavily dominant class naturally produces a high Expected Agreement, since chance alone, simply by predicting the common class often, already agrees with the true label frequently, exactly the situation that made raw accuracy so unreliable on imbalanced data in the first place, now made explicit and quantifiable through this calculation.

blocks.text: 5. Reading a Cohen Kappa Value
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061513-341774938.png

Cohen Kappa values have a clean, well-defined interpretation, though its scale reads differently from every other metric covered so far in this module. A value of exactly 1.0 represents perfect agreement, entirely beyond and independent of whatever chance alone would produce. A value of exactly 0.0 represents agreement no better than pure chance, regardless of whatever raw accuracy might otherwise suggest, exactly the correction this metric exists to provide.

A negative Cohen Kappa value indicates agreement genuinely worse than chance, a systematic pattern of disagreement between predictions and true labels, a serious warning sign worth investigating directly, echoing the same kind of red flag already covered for negative R² in the Model Evaluation Regression module. A more typical, moderately strong real-world value, somewhere between 0.6 and 0.8, indicates substantial agreement that is genuinely, meaningfully beyond what chance alone would explain, though still short of perfect.
6. Revisiting the Imbalanced-Data Example

It is worth returning directly to the exact imbalanced-data example first introduced in the Accuracy topic: a dataset with 99 percent negative examples and only 1 percent positive examples, where a trivial model that always predicts negative, completely ignoring every input feature, achieves a deceptively high 99 percent accuracy.

Computing Cohen Kappa for this exact same trivial model reveals the truth accuracy hid: since this model agrees with the true label no more, proportionally, than pure chance guessing would already be expected to achieve given the 99-to-1 class split, its Cohen Kappa comes out to exactly, or very close to, 0.0. This is a direct, concrete, numerical demonstration of exactly what Cohen Kappa exists to correct for, exposing a trivial, uninformative model that raw accuracy alone completely failed to flag.
7. Cohen Kappa's Original Purpose
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061513-649717757.png

It is worth understanding Cohen Kappa's original, historical purpose directly, since it clarifies why the metric is framed around agreement rather than correctness. Cohen Kappa was originally developed to measure agreement between two independent human annotators, or raters, evaluating the same set of items, not originally to compare a model's predictions against a single, objectively true label at all.

A classic example: two radiologists independently examining and diagnosing the same set of medical images. Cohen Kappa, in this original context, answers how much these two human experts genuinely agree with each other, beyond whatever level of agreement would be expected if both were essentially guessing randomly between the possible diagnoses. The exact same mathematical formula applies directly and equally well to comparing a model's predictions against a single set of true labels, simply treating the model as one of the two raters and the ground truth as the other, which is precisely how it gets used as a classification evaluation metric throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This inter-annotator-agreement framing is why Cohen Kappa remains especially popular in medical, psychological, and social science research, fields where measuring genuine agreement between human experts, beyond chance, is often just as important as, or more important than, evaluating a machine learning model against a fixed ground truth.

blocks.text: 8. A Common Reference Scale

A widely used, informal reference scale, commonly attributed to statisticians Landis and Koch, offers rough qualitative labels for different ranges of Cohen Kappa values, useful for quickly communicating what a given Kappa score roughly represents without requiring deep familiarity with the metric's exact mathematical definition.

Values from 0.0 to 0.20 are typically described as slight agreement, 0.21 to 0.40 as fair agreement, 0.41 to 0.60 as moderate agreement, 0.61 to 0.80 as substantial agreement, and 0.81 to 1.00 as almost perfect agreement. This scale is informal and somewhat field-dependent, worth treating as a rough communication convenience rather than a rigid, universally agreed-upon standard, but it remains a genuinely useful shorthand encountered frequently in research and applied reporting.

blocks.text: 9. When Cohen Kappa Is the Right Metric to Reach For

blocks.alt: When Cohen Kappa Is the Right Metric to Reach For
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061513-331240850.png

Cohen Kappa is the natural choice whenever comparing model quality across two or more datasets that have genuinely different class balances from each other, since its explicit chance-correction makes such comparisons fair and meaningful in a way that comparing raw accuracy scores across datasets with different class proportions simply cannot achieve, exactly the kind of unfair comparison plain accuracy is vulnerable to.

It remains the standard, natural choice whenever the actual task is evaluating agreement between two human labelers or annotators, rather than model predictions against a fixed ground truth, exactly its original, still-common historical use case. And it is a genuinely useful, direct check to run whenever there is suspicion that a reported accuracy figure might be artificially inflated by class imbalance, giving a precise, quantitative answer that a visual inspection of the class distribution alone cannot provide as cleanly.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes Cohen Kappa for the exact same trivial always-negative model from the Accuracy topic's worked example, directly exposing what its deceptively high accuracy hid.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score, accuracy_score

# The exact same 99-to-1 imbalanced setup from the Accuracy topic
actual = np.array([0] * 99 + [1])  # 99 negative, 1 positive, in this small illustrative sample

# A trivial model: always predicts negative, ignoring every feature entirely
trivial_predictions = np.zeros_like(actual)

trivial_accuracy = accuracy_score(actual, trivial_predictions)
trivial_kappa = cohen_kappa_score(actual, trivial_predictions)

print(f"Trivial always-negative model: accuracy={trivial_accuracy:.3f}, Cohen Kappa={trivial_kappa:.3f}")
print("Accuracy looks excellent; Cohen Kappa correctly reveals zero genuine skill beyond chance")

# A genuinely better model: correctly identifies the one positive case too
genuinely_better_predictions = actual.copy()
better_kappa = cohen_kappa_score(actual, genuinely_better_predictions)
better_accuracy = accuracy_score(actual, genuinely_better_predictions)
print(f"\nGenuinely perfect model: accuracy={better_accuracy:.3f}, Cohen Kappa={better_kappa:.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The trivial model's Cohen Kappa will come out at or very close to 0.0, exactly as expected, while its accuracy still looks deceptively high, a direct, numerical echo of the exact scenario first raised at the very start of this module in the Accuracy topic.

blocks.text: 11. Model Evaluation Classification Module Complete

This closes the Model Evaluation Classification module, ten topics building a complete toolkit for judging classifier quality from genuinely different, complementary angles: Accuracy's overall correctness, Precision and Recall's split view of positive-prediction quality, F1 Score's balanced combination of the two, the Confusion Matrix's complete underlying picture, Log Loss's evaluation of predicted probabilities directly, the ROC Curve and AUC's threshold-independent ranking view, the Precision-Recall Curve's imbalance-honest alternative, and finally Cohen Kappa's correction for chance agreement.

Every one of these ten metrics answers a genuinely different question about the same underlying classifier, and choosing which one, or which combination, to report depends directly on the specific problem's class balance, error costs, and whether raw labels or predicted probabilities matter most. The next module, Cross Validation, turns to a related but distinct question: not how to score a model's predictions, but how to reliably estimate that score in the first place, using data efficiently and honestly.
12. Key Takeaways

items: Cohen Kappa measures agreement between predictions and true labels, after subtracting out agreement chance alone would produce.
Observed Agreement is exactly accuracy; Expected Agreement quantifies how much chance alone would agree, given class proportions.
The formula normalizes the improvement over chance by the maximum possible improvement achievable given that same class distribution.
A value of 0 means no better than chance; negative values mean worse than chance, a serious warning sign.
Applied to the classic imbalanced-data trivial model, Cohen Kappa correctly scores 0, exposing what its 99 percent accuracy hid.
It was originally built to measure agreement between two human annotators, a use case still common in medical and social science research.
A common informal reference scale maps Kappa ranges to qualitative labels, from slight to almost perfect agreement.
It fits cross-dataset comparisons, human-annotator studies, and directly checking whether accuracy is inflated by class imbalance.
This closes the Model Evaluation Classification module; next up: Cross Validation, covering how to reliably estimate any of these metrics in the first place.
